passage: I'm Rekha, and that night I was the one on the status page. Every thirty minutes I posted a short update: what we knew, what we didn't, and when the next one would come. Zubin, who was leading the fix, sent me two lines at a time and I turned them into plain words. The first update said only, 'Payments are slow, we're looking into it, next update at nine forty.' Not glamorous, but at nine forty I posted again, even when the news was 'still working on it'. What surprised me was the support inbox. It had been flooding, and after the third update the messages slowed. One customer wrote, 'Thanks for actually telling us.' I was nervous the whole time, but I learned that people can bear bad news better than silence.

qa.q: How often did Rekha post an update?
qa.a: Rekha posted an update every thirty minutes.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel during the outage?
qa.a: Rekha was nervous the whole time, though the customer thanks brought some relief. 🙂

qa.q: What other approach could Rekha add if the cause stayed unknown for hours?
qa.a: Rekha could also message the biggest customers directly, since a public page may not be enough for people who depend on the service most.

qa.q: How might a customer have felt after reading the third update?
qa.a: A customer would likely feel calmer and respected, since one wrote 'Thanks for actually telling us.'

grounding: Shows a communications owner posting short honest updates on a regular schedule with the next update time, which eased customer worry.

passage: I'm Minakshi, and I work on the support phones. During last Thursday's outage, I watched something change. Usually, when the app goes down, our lines explode and we have nothing to tell anyone. This time Leela was named communications owner. At 4.10 she posted on the status page: 'Login is failing for many users. We're investigating. Next update 4.40.' At 4.40, exactly: 'Cause found in a database update. Fix being tested. Next update 5.10.' At 5.10: 'Fix rolling out. Some users may need to log in again.' She never promised a time she didn't know. I just read her updates to callers. Calls that normally peak at three hundred an hour stayed under ninety. I can't say whether Leela felt calm. Her posts did.

qa.a: 'Login is failing for many users. We're investigating. Next update 4.40.'

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt compared with past outages?
qa.a: Minakshi likely felt relieved and less helpless, finally having something honest to tell callers.

qa.q: What else could the team do with Leela's updates after the outage?
qa.a: They could save them as a template, so every communications owner posts at the same fixed rhythm.

qa.q: How might customers have experienced the thirty-minute updates?
qa.a: Knowing when the next update would come, customers had less reason to panic or call support.

grounding: It shows a colleague seeing a communications owner post short honest updates every thirty minutes with the next update time, reducing panic and support calls.

passage:
Tuesday, the first outage. The payments page is down for two hours. Nobody posts anything. Harish, who runs customer support, gets four hundred calls and has nothing to say except 'we're looking into it'.
Friday, the next week. Another outage, smaller. This time Tejas is named communications owner. He posts on the status page at 11.00: 'Some card payments failing. Cause not known yet. Next update 11.30.' At 11.30: 'Cause found. Fix in testing. Next update 12.00.' At 12.00: 'Fixed. Thank you for your patience.' Each one short, each one on time.
Monday. Harish brings a chart to the review. Friday's calls: sixty-five. 'Same kind of outage,' he says. 'The only difference is people knew when they'd hear from us.'

qa.q: How many calls did Harish's team get on Friday?
How might Harish have felt on the first Tuesday?
qa.a: Harish likely felt frustrated and helpless, taking four hundred calls with nothing to tell customers.

qa.q: What would make Tejas's updates even more useful next time?
qa.a: Posting the first update within minutes and adding what customers can do meanwhile, such as trying again later.

qa.q: How did customers experience Friday differently from Tuesday?
qa.a: On Friday they knew what was happening and when they'd hear next, so fewer felt the need to call.

grounding: It shows a communications owner posting short honest updates every thirty minutes with the next update time, which cuts panic and support calls.
